characterInteraction.description: The interviewer and Shirin Ebadi engage in a conversation about how globalization can be made more human-centered. Shirin Ebadi provides examples and detailed explanations.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Discussion on human-centered globalization and justice using Iran as an example.

narrativeProgression.description: Shirin Ebadi shares her views on how globalization can be made more human-centered, particularly emphasizing the need for the global establishment of justice. She uses Iran as an example, stating that in countries where courts lack independence, justice is absent. She recounts incidents following the 2009 Iranian presidential elections, where the government cracked down on its people, imprisoning, torturing, and killing many.

scenes.title: Human-Centered Globalization

characterInteraction.description: The interviewer and Shirin Ebadi continue their discussion, this time focusing on the Arab Spring and the potential for change in Iran. Shirin Ebadi expresses optimism for a democratic future in Iran but stresses the need for continued efforts and acknowledges the challenges involved.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Analysis of the Arab Spring's impact and technology's role in uniting people for change.

narrativeProgression.description: Shirin Ebadi discusses the Arab Spring and the role of technology in uniting people against oppressive regimes. She notes that despite successful uprisings in some countries, replacing one dictator with another is not a solution, and true progress requires more than just removing oppressive leaders.

scenes.thematicElements: Arab Spring, Technology, Democracy and Dictatorship
scenes.title: Impact of the Arab Spring and Technology

characterInteraction.description: The interviewer prompts Shirin Ebadi for her thoughts on the future of Iran. Shirin Ebadi responds with a hopeful outlook, underscoring the role of the younger generation, especially women, in pushing for democracy. She then ties her observations to the themes of globalization and justice discussed throughout the interview, reinforcing her stance on their interconnectedness.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Hopeful outlook on Iran's future, emphasizing the role of youth and women in achieving democracy.

narrativeProgression.description: Shirin Ebadi expresses hope for a democratic future in Iran, highlighting the potential of Iran's young population and, specifically, women and workers as a driving force for positive change. She connects this to the topic of the Zermatt Summit, stating that in addition to focusing on trade as a form of globalization, there must be other means pursued, including justice and ethics. She clarifies that human rights principles should be enforced universally, rejecting the idea of cultural relativism and emphasizing the need for a global perspective.

scenes.thematicElements: Hope for Iran, Women's Role, Globalization Beyond Trade
scenes.title: Hope for Iran's Future

climax.description: Hopeful outlook for Iran's democratic future.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: What do you think is the best way to put the human person back at the center of the globalization process?
Today we witness in globalization related only to trade.
We don't see any humanity so it is about time that humanity also entered globalization in all its aspects.
One of the things that must happen is establishment of justice. Justice must also become globalized.
In non-democratic countries where the courts do not have any independence, there is no justice.
For example, there is the case of Iran where after the presidential elections in 2009 there was a massive crackdown by the government.
Many people were imprisoned, tortured and killed. Therefore it is about time that justice became globalized because the courts in Iran as well paid no attention to the complaints made by the people.
If we globalize justice then non-democratic countries would also have to abide.
What do you think about the Arab Spring? Do you think it is all? Do you think we have to take it to transform it?
And to justice?
Both Muslim people in the Arab world have become tired of the sporty groups.
And there was such a strong censorship in the Arab world that people had no access to news of what was going on in the rest of the world.
Because of that they could not unite because they didn't know what was going on in the outside world.
Technology came to the aid of the Muslim Arabs and they managed to stage uprising against the dictators.
And two of these Arab countries fortunately managed to topple the dictators.
But this is not enough. Just toppling dictators is not enough.
If you look at our history in 1979 we managed to topple the dictators but one dictator was replaced with another.
Do you have any hope for Iran?
I very much hope that democracy will come to Iran in not too distant future because Iran has much potential to become the democratic country.
But let's not forget that 70% of the Iranian population around the age of 30 and especially the women and workers in Iran are good potential labor force for bringing democracy into the country.
Yes, the women played a very neutral especially in Iran as you've seen from the footage and the pictures that have been around.
Women have had a very strong press and especially in the street demonstration.
It was a woman who became symbol of the green movement of democracy in Iran, a woman called Netta who was shot by the security forces.
Five minutes after she was shot the footage of that was spread all over the world.
The topic of the summit has been extremely good and I think in addition to focusing on trade as a way of globalization there must be other ways that should be pursued.
As I mentioned earlier justice should also be able to apply and also ethics is something else which should be able to apply.
These days we witnessed that many people are talking about the idea of cultural relativism and they're saying that human rights and cultural relativism should be related to the world.
I think that human rights and all the human rights principles should be enforced and cultural relativism should not play a part in that it should be global.

youtube_description:
Exclusive interview - after her talk at the Zermatt Summit  on Women: actors of change.
Shirin Ebadi J.D. was awarded the 2003 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote human rights, especially those of women, children and political prisoners in Iran. She was the first Muslim woman to have received the Nobel Peace Prize, and only the fifth to win the award in any field. Dr Ebadi was one of the first female judges in Iran. She served as president of the city court of Tehran from 1975 to 1979 and was the first Iranian woman to achieve Chief Justice status. After dismissal in wake of the Islamic Revolution in 1979, she was made a clerk in the court she once presided over, until petitioning for early retirement. After obtaining her lawyer's license in 1992, Dr Ebadi set up private practice and defended numerous political dissidents resulting in her arrest on many occasions. She has also established many non-governmental organizations in Iran, including the Million Signatures Campaign to demand an end to legal discrimination against women in Iranian law. Dr Ebadi is a university professor and has published 13 books and over 70 articles dedicated to human rights. In 2004, she was named by Forbes Magazine as one of the world's 100 most powerful women
